title: Call to subsidise property cover in hard-hit regions
full_text:
Natural disasters Premiums are unaffordable for many, and under-insurance can lead to severe financial hardship, writes Sian Powell.
Subsidised property insurance is an important way to address the increasingly urgent problem of ballooning property insurance costs in high-risk regions, according to experts in the field.
A scheme of that nature would keep homeowners in the insurance net but it would affect the price signal, says Paula Jarzabkowski, professor of strategic management at the University of Queensland Business School.
Dealing with the loss of the price signal would require further decisions, she told the Financial Review Insurance Summit in Sydney in June. "Then we have a cascading trade-off," she said. "It's not a single decision."
The increasing frequency and severity of natural disasters such as floods and bushfires has led to soaring property insurance premiums in hard-hit regional districts. Fifteen per cent of properties in regional areas are now exposed to "unaffordable" insurance premiums - higher than one month of the owners' income, Actuaries Institute chief executive Elayne Grace said.
"Obviously in some regional areas it's a lot more. It can be up to 60 per cent that flows through," she added, noting the high insurance premiums are depressing property prices.
Jarzabkowski and her University of Queensland colleagues this year released a paper titled Building Resilience: Linking Disaster Insurance and Risk Mitigation for a Sustainable future.
The report says that without insurance, the cost of clean-ups, temporary accommodation and rebuilding fall directly on household savings and government expenditure, potentially causing extreme financial hardship.
Principles used in France, including modelling on how to limit the government's liability, could be applied in Australia, Jarzabkowski told The Australian Financial Review.
A national risk and resilience rating system is a key recommendation of the Housing Resilience Action Plan 2030, a report by Monash academics, the Financial Rights Legal Centre, the Resilient Building Council and others. The RBC has already conducted more than 63,000 home assessments, said Julia Davis, senior policy and communications officer at the Financial Rights Legal Centre. The council also offers a free bushfire app to help property owners self-assess risk.
"Fifty per cent of the general insurance market already gives discounts on these resilience ratings," she said.
An overarching national risk assessment agreement between banks, insurers, investors and community groups is the way forward, she added. "We know that banks and insurers and households need a common language for how we're going to assess risk, how we're going to assess resilience."
Over time, the effectiveness of resilience ratings and how much they reduce the cost of loss will become clear, she said. They should not be seen as a magical way to immediately reduce property insurance premiums. Rather, they are tools to help consumers "prevent their premium from doubling every year".AFR
